0.title: God with His People
0.essay:
The Bible begins with God walking with man in a garden. It ends with God living among his people in a city, where “they will see his face” (Revelation 22:4). Everything in between is the story of how the one became the other.

One thread

Read the Bible quickly from beginning to end and a single line runs through it. God makes a world and puts the man and woman in a garden where he meets them. They sin and are sent out. Then God comes after them. He lives in a tent among the tribes of Israel, then in a temple in Jerusalem. The glory leaves, and the people go into exile. Then the eternal Son takes flesh and lives among us, and his name is Immanuel, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23). He dies, the temple curtain is torn, and he pours out his Spirit, so that his people themselves become God’s house. At the last a voice from the throne says, “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3).

The words change from age to age: garden, tabernacle, temple, Christ, church, city. The purpose never changes. God says it again and again, from Leviticus to Revelation: “I will make my dwelling among you … and will be your God, and you shall be my people” (Leviticus 26:11–12).

Why it matters

This thread tells us who we are. We were made for God’s presence, to know him, enjoy him and live before his face. It tells us what sin is: not only breaking rules, but being sent out from the place where we belong. And it tells us what salvation is: being brought home to God.

The study The Big Story of the Bible traces the whole plot of Scripture. This study follows one golden thread in it, and finds it ending, as everything does, in Jesus Christ.

The chapters

The Garden Where God Walked; A Tent in the Wilderness; The Temple and the Departing Glory; Immanuel; The Spirit and the Living Temple; and The City Where God Lives.

For reflection

Where do you feel most “at home” in life, and where do you feel most out of place? What would it mean for you to believe that you were made to live in God’s presence?

1.title: The Garden Where God Walked
1.essay:
The first home of humanity was not simply a pleasant park. It was the place where God came to be with the people he had made. Eden was the first sanctuary, and the first loss was the loss of God’s presence.

A garden planted by God

In six days God made heaven and earth and all that is in them, and everything was “very good”. Then, as Genesis 2 tells it more closely, “the LORD God planted a garden in Eden, in the east, and there he put the man whom he had formed” (Genesis 2:8). The garden was full of trees “pleasant to the sight and good for food”, and in the middle stood “the tree of life” (Genesis 2:9). God gave the man work: he put him there “to work it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). God did not make man and then leave him. He made a place and put him in it, close to himself.

The most moving line comes after things have gone wrong. The man and woman “heard the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day” (Genesis 3:8). The words assume this was not new. God came. He walked where they lived. Life in Eden was life in company with God.

The first sanctuary

A sanctuary is a holy place set apart where God meets his people. Scripture never calls Eden a temple in so many words, but the later sanctuaries are full of Eden, and many Bible readers have seen that Eden was the first.

Look at the echoes. The verb for God “walking” in the garden is the one God later uses for his presence in the tabernacle: “I will walk among you and will be your God” (Leviticus 26:12). The pair of Hebrew verbs used for Adam’s task, to work and keep, is used together again for the Levites, who served and guarded the tabernacle (Numbers 3:7–8). Adam was a gardener, but he was also something like a priest.

There is more. Eden’s land had gold and onyx (Genesis 2:12), and gold and onyx stones later adorned the tabernacle and the high priest. Solomon carved the walls of the temple with “cherubim and palm trees and open flowers” (1 Kings 6:29), so that going in was like walking back into a garden. And Ezekiel, speaking of the king of Tyre, calls Eden “the garden of God” and “the holy mountain of God” in the same breath (Ezekiel 28:13–14). Eden, it seems, sat on a height, and a river flowed out of it to water the earth, as later a river flows out of the temple in Ezekiel’s vision (Ezekiel 47:1).

Sent out to the east

Then came the fall. The serpent lied, the woman and the man ate, and the first thing they did afterwards was hide: they “hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden” (Genesis 3:8). The friend had become a threat. Shame and fear had entered the world.

God called, “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9). That is not the question of someone who does not know. Even in judgment God spoke a promise: the offspring of the woman would crush the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15). But the sentence still fell. “The LORD God sent him out from the garden of Eden.” And “at the east of the garden of Eden he placed the cherubim and a flaming sword that turned every way to guard the way to the tree of life” (Genesis 3:23–24).

Cherubim are mighty heavenly creatures who in Scripture guard and attend God’s holy presence. Notice where they stand: on the east side. From then on, the entrance to God’s house faces east. The tabernacle court opened to the east (Exodus 27:13). Golden cherubim stood over the ark, and cherubim were woven into the curtain before the Most Holy Place (Exodus 26:31). Every Israelite who looked at that curtain was looking, in a sense, at the gate of Eden, still guarded, still shut.

What exile from God means

This is the heart of the human problem. Sin is not merely a bad habit or a broken rule. It is separation from God. Isaiah says it plainly: “your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God” (Isaiah 59:2). Every human being since has been born east of Eden: alive, gifted, made in God’s image, and yet far from home.

This explains much of our experience. We try to fill the emptiness with work, pleasure, relationships, success. These are often good gifts, but they cannot be the presence of God. We are homesick for a place we have never seen.

And yet the God who walked in the garden did not stop walking. The whole Bible is the story of his coming after us. The way back past the cherubim would one day be opened, not by our climbing over the gate but by the promised offspring of the woman bearing the flaming sword himself. Christ took the judgment that kept us out, so that he could bring us in.

An example

A man in his fifties had done well by every outward measure: career, house, family. Yet he described a constant low hum of restlessness, as if he had missed a train he could not name. Reading Genesis 3 with a friend, he stopped at the words “Where are you?” He said quietly that he had been hiding for thirty years. It was the start of his coming home. He found that God had been calling after him all along.

For reflection

What do you notice when you read Genesis 2–3 as the story of a sanctuary? In what ways do people still “hide” from God? Where do you see in your own heart the homesickness of someone born east of Eden? How does it help to know that God came looking for Adam?

2.title: A Tent in the Wilderness
2.essay:
God rescued Israel from Egypt, and almost at once he told them to build him a tent. He did not want only to save them from slavery. He wanted to live among them.

“That I may dwell in their midst”

At Mount Sinai God gave Moses careful instructions: “let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst” (Exodus 25:8). That sentence is the reason for the whole tabernacle. A tabernacle is a tent, here a portable sanctuary of curtains and wooden frames, which Israel carried through the wilderness and set up at the centre of the camp. God even says that this was why he had saved them: he “brought them out of the land of Egypt that I might dwell among them” (Exodus 29:46).

The tabernacle had an outer court with an altar and a washing basin, then a tent in two rooms. The first was the Holy Place, with the lampstand, the table of bread and the altar of incense. The inner room was the Most Holy Place (sometimes called the Holy of Holies). In it stood the ark of the covenant, a gold-covered chest holding the tablets of the law, covered by a lid called the mercy seat with two golden cherubim over it. God said, “There I will meet with you” (Exodus 25:22).

The Hebrew word for tabernacle, mishkan, comes from the verb “to dwell”. Later Jewish teachers used a related word, Shekinah, for God’s dwelling presence, the glory that settled among his people. The word is not in the Bible, but the reality is.

The glory came down

When the work was finished, something astonishing happened. “Then the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. And Moses was not able to enter the tent of meeting because the cloud settled on it” (Exodus 40:34–35). The God who had walked in Eden had come to live among his people again. The cloud by day and fire by night stayed over the tent “in the sight of all the house of Israel throughout all their journeys” (Exodus 40:38). Wherever Israel camped, God camped with them.

The golden calf and Moses’ plea

But between the instructions and the building came a disaster. While Moses was on the mountain, the people said to Aaron, “Up, make us gods who shall go before us” (Exodus 32:1), and they bowed to a golden calf. They wanted a god they could see and handle and control. It was Eden again: the people God had come to live with turned away from him.

God’s answer is chilling. He would still give them the land, “but I will not go up among you, lest I consume you on the way” (Exodus 33:3). They could have the gifts without the Giver. Moses would not. He prayed, “If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here” (Exodus 33:15). The land without God was not worth having. What marked Israel out was not their land or their law, but this: “Is it not in your going with us, so that we are distinct, I and your people, from every other people on the face of the earth?” (Exodus 33:16).

And God, in mercy, said yes: “My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest” (Exodus 33:14). Then he passed before Moses and proclaimed his name: “The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). The God who comes to live with sinners does so because this is who he is.

Near, yet only by blood

Yet the tabernacle also taught that God’s presence is dangerous to sinners. Moses asked to see God’s glory and was told, “you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live” (Exodus 33:20). A thick curtain, the veil, hung between the Holy Place and the Most Holy, “with cherubim skillfully worked into it” (Exodus 26:31). Even the high priest could not come in “at any time … so that he may not die” (Leviticus 16:2). Only once a year, on the Day of Atonement, could he go in, and “not without taking blood” (Hebrews 9:7).

So the tabernacle preached two things at once. God is near: he lives in the middle of the camp. And God is holy: sinners cannot simply walk in. Every sacrifice at the altar said that the way to God is through a death in the place of the sinner. The letter to the Hebrews says the Holy Spirit was teaching by all this “that the way into the holy places is not yet opened as long as the first section is still standing” (Hebrews 9:8).

Here is the gospel in shadow. The tabernacle was a copy of something greater (Hebrews 9:24). The blood of bulls and goats pointed forward to the blood of the Lamb of God. God was preparing his people to understand a Saviour who would be both the place where God meets us and the sacrifice that makes the meeting safe.

An example

A young woman was offered a promotion that would have meant moving to a town with no faithful church and long Sunday shifts. Everyone told her it was a gift from God. She read Exodus 33 and found herself praying Moses’ words. She did not think every move away from a church is wrong, but she saw that she had been weighing salary and status and had not weighed the presence of God at all. She stayed, and later found a role that let her keep her place among God’s people.

For reflection

Why do you think God wanted to live among Israel rather than simply guide them from a distance? Are there ways you are tempted to want God’s gifts without God himself? What does the veil teach about God’s holiness? How does the tabernacle help you see why Christ had to die?

3.title: The Temple and the Departing Glory
3.essay:
In the land God gave them, Israel built him a house of stone. The glory came down, the psalmists sang of their longing to be near, and then, because of the people’s sin, the glory went away.

Solomon’s temple

For centuries God lived in a tent, “moving about in a tent for my dwelling” (2 Samuel 7:6). Then Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem. Its plan followed the tabernacle, only larger and more splendid. The inner sanctuary, the Most Holy Place, was a perfect cube, “twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high” and covered in pure gold (1 Kings 6:20). Remember that shape; we will meet it again at the end of the Bible.

At the dedication the glory came down as it had at Sinai. “A cloud filled the house of the LORD, so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD” (1 Kings 8:10–11).

Yet Solomon knew a building could not hold God. “But will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built!” (1 Kings 8:27). God is everywhere, filling heaven and earth (Jeremiah 23:24). But he chose to be present in a special way, to bless and to hear, in one place among one people. Solomon’s prayer asked that God would hear prayers made “toward this place” and, when he heard, would “forgive” (1 Kings 8:30). The temple was above all a place of mercy.

The longing of the psalms

The temple became the focus of Israel’s love. The psalms are full of this longing. “How lovely is your dwelling place, O LORD of hosts! My soul longs, yes, faints for the courts of the LORD” (Psalm 84:1–2). “For a day in your courts is better than a thousand elsewhere” (Psalm 84:10). And far from it, they wept: “When shall I come and appear before God?” (Psalm 42:2). David’s great desire was not a building but a Person: “One thing have I asked of the LORD, that will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze upon the beauty of the LORD” (Psalm 27:4).

The glory departs

God had warned Solomon that if Israel turned to other gods, he would cast the house “out of my sight” (1 Kings 9:7). Over the following centuries they did exactly that. Idols were set up even inside the temple courts. God showed the prophet Ezekiel what was happening and called it what it was: abominations committed “to drive me far from my sanctuary” (Ezekiel 8:6).

Then Ezekiel saw one of the saddest sights in Scripture. The glory of the LORD rose from above the cherubim and moved to the threshold of the house (Ezekiel 10:4). It went out and paused “at the entrance of the east gate” (Ezekiel 10:19). Then “the glory of the LORD went up from the midst of the city and stood on the mountain that is on the east side of the city” (Ezekiel 11:23). Slowly, reluctantly, as if looking back, God left. And he left to the east, the same direction Adam had gone out of Eden.

The judgment followed. In 586 BC the Babylonians “burned the house of God and broke down the wall of Jerusalem” (2 Chronicles 36:19), and the people were taken away into exile. It was Eden all over again: sin, and banishment from God’s presence.

Yet even then God did not abandon his scattered people. He promised, “I have been a sanctuary to them for a while in the countries where they have gone” (Ezekiel 11:16).

The promised return

Then came the promise. Ezekiel saw a new temple, and “the glory of the God of Israel was coming from the east” (Ezekiel 43:2). It entered by the east gate, “and behold, the glory of the LORD filled the temple” (Ezekiel 43:5). God said, “this is the place of my throne … where I will dwell in the midst of the people of Israel forever” (Ezekiel 43:7). The book ends with the name of the city: “The LORD Is There” (Ezekiel 48:35).

After the exile the people came back and rebuilt the temple. But it was a poor thing beside Solomon’s, and the old men who remembered the first house wept (Ezra 3:12). No cloud of glory is recorded filling it. Still God promised through Haggai, “The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former” (Haggai 2:9). And Malachi said, “the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple” (Malachi 3:1). How could that be? The answer would walk into that very temple as a baby in his mother’s arms.

Will there be another temple?

Christians differ over Ezekiel’s temple vision (Ezekiel 40–48). Many dispensationalists believe it describes a future temple to be built in Jerusalem, often with sacrifices offered as memorials of Christ’s death, because they read its detailed measurements as describing a real building.

This commentary’s view: the New Testament never expects a rebuilt temple or renewed sacrifice. Hebrews teaches that Christ’s sacrifice was offered “once for all” (Hebrews 9:12), and returning to animal sacrifice would seem to go backwards. Ezekiel’s vision is a picture, drawn in the language Israel knew, of God dwelling with his people for ever. It is fulfilled in Christ, in his church, and finally in the new Jerusalem, where John says, “I saw no temple in the city” (Revelation 21:22). The river from Ezekiel’s temple flows again in Revelation 22.

An example

An elderly woman, no longer able to get to church, told her minister that Psalm 84 made her cry. She had sung it for years, and now she was shut out of the courts she loved. He reminded her of Ezekiel 11:16: the God who was a sanctuary to exiles in Babylon was a sanctuary to her in her flat. She still longed for the gathered church, and rightly. But she stopped feeling forgotten.

For reflection

What does Solomon’s question in 1 Kings 8:27 teach you about God? Which line of Psalm 84 or Psalm 27 most expresses your own longing? Why did the glory leave the temple, and what does that warn us about? How do the promises of Ezekiel and Haggai prepare us to meet Jesus?

4.title: Immanuel
4.essay:
Everything the tabernacle and temple pictured came true in a person. In Jesus Christ, God did not merely visit his people in a cloud. He became one of them.

God with us

Seven centuries before Christ, Isaiah gave a sign to a faithless king: “Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel” (Isaiah 7:14). Matthew tells us what that name means and to whom it belongs. When Mary conceived by the Holy Spirit, this was fulfilled: “they shall call his name Immanuel (which means, God with us)” (Matthew 1:23).

The name is not just a hope that God would be on our side. It describes who the child is. Jesus is God the Son, the second person of the Trinity, who took a true human nature without ceasing to be God. In him “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9). The promise “I will dwell in your midst” (Zechariah 2:10) is kept in a stable in Bethlehem.

The Word tabernacled among us

John says it in temple language: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). The Greek verb translated “dwelt” means to pitch a tent. John is saying, in effect, that the Word tabernacled among us. The glory that filled the tent in the wilderness was now seen in a human face.

And notice the words “full of grace and truth”. They echo the name God proclaimed to Moses, “abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). Moses was told he could not see God’s face. John says, “No one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known” (John 1:18). To see Jesus is to see “the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

This is how the promise of Haggai came true. The latter glory of the house was greater than the former, not because the stones were finer, but because the Lord of the temple walked into it.

The true temple

Jesus knew this about himself. He said, “something greater than the temple is here” (Matthew 12:6). When he drove the traders out of the temple courts and was challenged, he answered, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” His hearers thought of the building, which had “taken forty-six years to build”. “But he was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 2:19–21).

Jesus is the place where God and man meet. He is what the tabernacle and temple were pointing to all along. So he told the Samaritan woman that the hour was coming “when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father” (John 4:21). True worship would no longer depend on a building in one city, but on coming to the Father through the Son by the Spirit. This is why the New Testament has no interest in a holy site or a holy building. It has a holy Person.

The curtain torn

But how could sinners come to this Holy One? The answer is at the cross. As Jesus died, “Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and yielded up his spirit. And behold, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:50–51).

That curtain, woven with cherubim, had hung between sinners and God’s presence for centuries, as the cherubim had guarded the way into Eden. Now it was torn, and torn from the top, as by the hand of God. The way in was open. Hebrews explains it: “since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh … let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith” (Hebrews 10:19–22).

His body was torn so that the veil could be torn. He was shut out, crying, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46), so that we could be brought in. He bore the flaming sword of God’s judgment so that we could pass the cherubim and eat of the tree of life. “In Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13).

What a Saviour! The God whom no one could see without dying chose to die so that we could see him and live.

Drawing near today

This changes how a Christian prays. We do not stand outside the curtain hoping a priest will speak for us. We have “a great priest over the house of God” (Hebrews 10:21), and so we may “with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16). The person who has trusted Christ is welcome in the Most Holy Place every day, not because they are good enough, but because his blood has made the way.

An example

A teenager raised in church thought of prayer as something like knocking on the door of a head teacher’s office: polite, nervous, best kept short. A youth leader walked him through Hebrews 10 and the torn curtain. He said later that it was the first time he understood that he was not outside the room at all. He began to pray as a son speaks to a father who wants him there.

For reflection

What does the name Immanuel mean to you in the place you are in now? How does John 1:14 change the way you read the tabernacle? Why does it matter that the curtain was torn from top to bottom? What keeps you from drawing near to God with confidence, and how does Hebrews 10 answer it?

5.title: The Spirit and the Living Temple
5.essay:
Jesus rose and ascended to the Father. But he did not leave his people alone. He sent the Holy Spirit, and through the Spirit God now lives in his people. The church is his temple.

“We will come to him and make our home with him”

On the night before he died, Jesus told his disciples he was going away. They were troubled. So he promised them “another Helper, to be with you forever, even the Spirit of truth … for he dwells with you and will be in you. I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you” (John 14:16–18). Then he said something even more astonishing: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him” (John 14:23).

Think of what this means. The God whose glory filled the tabernacle, the God before whom priests could not stand, makes his home with an ordinary believer. Father, Son and Holy Spirit come to live with the one who loves Jesus. This is not a reward for the especially holy. It is true of every Christian. “Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9), so everyone who belongs to him has the Spirit.

Fire on the new temple

At Pentecost the promise came true. There came “a sound like a mighty rushing wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting. And divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:2–4). When the tabernacle and temple were finished, God’s glory came down in cloud and fire. Now the fire rested not on a building but on people. The new temple had been dedicated.

The church is God’s temple

So the apostles speak of the church in temple language. Paul writes to the Corinthian church, “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16). He tells Gentile believers, once outsiders, that they are “members of the household of God … being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:19, 22). Christ is the cornerstone, the apostles and prophets the foundation, and every believer is part of the building. Peter says the same: “you yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood” (1 Peter 2:5).

Paul even takes God’s old promise from Leviticus and applies it to the church: “For we are the temple of the living God; as God said, ‘I will make my dwelling among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people’” (2 Corinthians 6:16). The God who walked in Eden walks among his gathered people.

The temple is first of all the church together. But Paul also says it of each believer’s body: “do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). The study The Holy Spirit treats his work in us more fully.

What this means for everyday life

Worship. We do not need a holy city or a special building to meet God. We come to the Father through Christ wherever we are. And yet the gathered church matters more, not less, because it is there that God has promised to live in a special way. When believers meet in his name, Christ is “among them” (Matthew 18:20). Hebrews tells us not to neglect meeting together (Hebrews 10:25). Sunday worship is not an optional extra to private faith; it is the temple gathering.

Holiness. “God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Corinthians 3:17). Paul said this to a church divided by factions and stained by sexual sin. If God lives in us, how we treat our bodies and one another matters. But notice the order. Paul does not say, “Become holy so that God will live in you.” He says, “God lives in you, so live like it.” The command rests on the gift.

Loneliness. Many people, Christians included, feel deeply alone. The Bible does not dismiss that; even Jesus wanted his friends near in Gethsemane. But a believer is never abandoned. Christ’s promise stands: “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). And God has given the lonely a household, a family of brothers and sisters in whom his Spirit lives. If loneliness has settled into a heavy, lasting low mood, it is wise to speak to a doctor as well as a pastor; that is no failure of faith.

The gathered church. If the church is God’s temple, then tearing it apart by gossip and division is serious, and building it up is holy work. The smallest act of welcome, the newcomer greeted, the visit to the sick, is laying living stones.

An example

A widower in his seventies stopped going to church after his wife died. Sitting alone in the pew they had shared was too hard, and he thought he could pray just as well at home. A younger couple began to sit with him, and then to invite him for Sunday lunch. Some months later he said he had learned that God lived not only in his heart but among his people, and that he had needed both.

For reflection

How does it change your view of yourself to know that Father, Son and Spirit have made their home with you? Why do you think the New Testament speaks of the church together as God’s temple? Where is God calling you to holiness because you are his temple? Who in your church might feel alone, and how could you help?

6.title: The City Where God Lives
6.essay:
The story ends where it was always going: God and his people together, face to face, for ever. Eden is not simply restored. It is surpassed.

“The dwelling place of God is with man”

In the last chapters of the Bible, John sees “a new heaven and a new earth” and “the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God”. Then he hears the sentence the whole Bible has been waiting for: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God” (Revelation 21:1–3).

The word translated “dwelling place” is the Greek word for a tent, the word used for the tabernacle. Every earlier dwelling, the garden, the tent, the temple, the Word made flesh, the church, was leading here. The promise first given at Sinai, “I … will be your God, and you shall be my people” (Leviticus 26:12), is spoken a final time, and now nothing will ever break it.

And what follows is tender. “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away” (Revelation 21:4). God’s presence does not only mean glory. It means comfort.

No temple, because God is there

John then says something surprising for a Jew: “I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb” (Revelation 21:22). There is no building, because none is needed. The whole city is filled with God. There is no curtain, no inner room closed off. “The glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Revelation 21:23).

Look at the shape of the city. “Its length and width and height are equal” (Revelation 21:16), and “the city was pure gold” (Revelation 21:18). It is a cube of gold, like the Most Holy Place in Solomon’s temple, only vast. The whole of the new creation has become the Most Holy Place. Where once only the high priest could go, once a year, with blood, now all God’s people live, for ever, through the blood of the Lamb.

This is why this commentary does not look for a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem. The goal of every temple was never a building but God living with his people, and that goal is reached in Christ and in the city where God and the Lamb are the temple.

Eden restored and surpassed

The last chapter takes us back to the garden. “The river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb” runs through the city, and on either side is “the tree of life” (Revelation 22:1–2). The way that the cherubim guarded is open, and its fruit is for all who belong to Christ. Jesus had promised, “To the one who conquers I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God” (Revelation 2:7).

“No longer will there be anything accursed” (Revelation 22:3). The curse of Genesis 3 is lifted. But this is more than a return to the beginning. Eden was a garden for two; this is a city for a multitude from every nation. In Eden man could fall; here nothing unclean will ever enter (Revelation 21:27), and those who are there are kept for ever. Eden had a serpent; here the serpent has been thrown down. And in Eden God walked with man; here God and the Lamb sit on the throne in the middle of the city.

“They will see his face”

The crown of it all is four words: “They will see his face” (Revelation 22:4). Moses was told, “you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live” (Exodus 33:20). Now God’s servants will see him and live, and live as never before. “Now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12). “We shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

This is the end for which we were made. The psalmist said, “in your presence there is fullness of joy” (Psalm 16:11). Heaven is not chiefly a place of pleasant rest, though it is restful. It is being with God. Jesus prayed for exactly this: “Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory” (John 17:24).

What a God, who would go to such lengths, from the garden to the cross, so that people who hid from him could see his face with joy.

Hope for now

This future reaches back into the present. Those who die in Christ go at once to be “at home with the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:8), awaiting the resurrection and the new creation. The study Death, Dying & Heaven says more about this.

For the suffering, it means that tears are real but temporary, and that God himself will wipe them away. For the lonely, it means that the deepest companionship is still ahead, and that even now the God who will dwell with us is with us. For the homesick, it means that the ache is not foolish. You were made for this city. And for the one who has not yet come to Christ, it means the door stands open. The curtain is torn. The Lamb who is the temple of the city still says, “Come.”

An example

A nurse on a cancer ward kept a card with Revelation 21:3–4 on it in her pocket. Some patients she cared for were believers, and she would sometimes read it to them near the end. One woman, very weak, asked her to read it twice. Then she said, “So I’m not going away. I’m going home.” The nurse has never forgotten it.

For reflection

What strikes you most about the picture of the new Jerusalem in Revelation 21–22? Why do you think there is no temple in the city? What would it mean for you to see God’s face? How might this hope change the way you face suffering, loneliness or death this week?
